title: Best Gym and Cross-Training Shoes UK
short: Cross-training shoes compared by stability, cushioning and fit, for lifting, HIIT and mixed gym workouts.
intro: A cross-training shoe has to do several jobs at once: stay stable under a heavy squat, flex for burpees, and hold up on a short run. This guide compares shoes tested by BarBend, covering the best options for lifting, HIIT, wide and flat feet, and barefoot-style training.

products.name: Nano X5
products.best_for: Mixed workouts combining strength training and cardio
products.key_spec: Updated EVA midsole, rope climb traction plate
products.summary: BarBend's overall pick. An updated EVA midsole supports running better than previous Nanos, with a rope climb traction plate and a wide colour range, though the Flexweave upper stretches over time and there's no wide sizing.

products.name: Metcon 9
products.best_for: Wider-footed lifters who prioritise strength work
products.key_spec: Wider toe box, durable mesh upper, 13.55oz
products.summary: A wider toe box than previous Metcons with a durable mesh upper and extensive rope guard, though BarBend found it heavy and the rigid plate limits cardio performance.
pros: Wider toe box than previous versions

products.name: Adipower Weightlifting 3
products.best_for: Olympic lifters and back squat specialists
products.key_spec: 22mm heel-drop, wider heel, multiple closure systems
products.summary: A dedicated weightlifting shoe with a 22mm heel-drop that aids squat positioning and a wider heel for stability, though it has a narrow toe box and limited versatility outside lifting.

products.name: Outwork Edge Series
products.best_for: Flat-footed athletes who need extra stability
products.summary: A sturdy heel counter and herringbone outsole that maintains traction, well suited to flat-footed lifters, though the upper lacks breathability and needs an extended break-in period.
cons: High-tops difficult to put on and remove

products.name: F-Lite G 300
products.summary: A lightweight shoe with a graphene-infused outsole BarBend rates as extremely durable, plus a dedicated rope-grip system, though eyelets are prone to tearing and the collar fits tight.

products.name: Fuse 3.0
products.best_for: Budget-conscious gym-goers who still lift heavy
products.summary: Excellent value with a quick break-in and a stable midsole well suited to heavy lifts, though colour choice is limited and the 4mm drop can feel flat for some.
pros: Stable midsole ideal for heavy lifts

products.name: Prio
products.best_for: Buyers who want a zero-drop, minimalist training shoe
products.summary: A zero-drop minimalist shoe with a removable insole, affordable and durable, though it has a learning curve if you haven't trained barefoot-style before.

products.name: One v2
products.best_for: High-intensity interval training with multidirectional movement
products.summary: BarBend picks this for HIIT, with a 6mm drop that balances lifting and sprinting and a durable build, though it's premium-priced and sizing can be inconsistent for wider feet.

guide.q: What heel-to-toe drop should I look for?
guide.a: A lower drop (zero to 4mm) suits lifting and barefoot-style training by keeping your heel close to the ground. A slightly higher drop (6mm or so) is a good compromise for mixed HIIT sessions that include running. Dedicated weightlifting shoes often use a much higher, fixed heel (around 20mm+) specifically to aid squat depth and posture.

guide.q: Do I need a dedicated weightlifting shoe?
guide.a: If you regularly do heavy back squats or Olympic lifts, a weightlifting shoe's raised, stable heel can improve your position. For general gym training, HIIT and mixed workouts, a cross-trainer with a lower, more versatile drop is usually more practical.

guide.q: Can I run in cross-training shoes?
guide.a: Cross-trainers can handle short runs and sprints within a workout, but their firmer, more stable build makes them less cushioned and comfortable than a dedicated running shoe over longer distances.

guide.q: How do I choose between stability and flexibility?
guide.a: Heavier lifting benefits from a firmer, more stable shoe that won't compress under load. More dynamic training, like HIIT or plyometrics, benefits from a shoe with more flex and cushioning. Several picks here specialise in one or the other, so match the shoe to what you do most.
